Homemade Aloe Vera Soap Using the Hot Pr.detailed_instructions:
1. Add the oils to a crock pot (or a dedicated heavy-based saucepan): 75g cocoa butter, 300g olive oil, 225g rice bran oil (can substitute more olive oil), 150g coconut oil. Turn the crock pot to HIGH for 5-10 minutes to melt the cocoa butter; if using a saucepan use only VERY low heat and switch the stove on/off as needed - 80C/180F is the maximum temperature for hot process soap.
2. Prepare 50g fresh aloe vera gel, blended completely smooth with no chunks or lumps; weigh into a separate container and set aside. (The recipe also works with the aloe omitted.)
3. Wearing goggles and gloves, prepare the lye solution: 200g filtered tap water (author used half ice to reduce fumes) and 100g sodium hydroxide. For a harder, drier soap usable sooner, use 150g water instead of 200g. Set the solution somewhere safe.
4. Prepare optional essential oils and colourant: 20g tea tree essential oil plus 10g eucalyptus essential oil weighed together in a small jar, and 3 tsp French green clay.
5. Blend the clay into the melted oils.
6. Add the lye solution to the oils and stick blend until the batter starts to emulsify.
7. Add the aloe vera gel and keep blending - the mixture becomes very thick.
8. When too thick to blend, remove the stick blender, scrape down the sides, and cover the pot with a lid.
9. Cook on low/very low heat for 15-20 minutes until the soap darkens and goes through gel phase; with a saucepan you may need to turn the burner off entirely - keep the soap at or below 80C/180F (an infra-red thermometer is handy).
10. When the soap looks vaseline-like, test with pH strips to confirm saponification is complete; cook longer on very low/no heat if not yet done.
11. Remove from heat, cool 5-10 minutes (no hotter than 80C/180F) and stir in the essential oils.
12. Spoon the soap into the mould, banging it down regularly to avoid air pockets.
13. Let the soap cool and harden in the mould for 1-3 days, then unmould and cut into bars.
14. Cure/dry for 4 weeks before using - even hot process soap should be properly cured for mildness and a hard, dry bar.
Homemade Aloe Vera Soap Using the Hot Pr.extra_notes: Recipe specs: 750g total soaping oils, 5% superfat, 2:1 water-to-lye ratio (2.5:1 once aloe is counted); mould holds ~1100g (1.1kg / 2.4 lb) of batter. Safety: goggles and gloves throughout; site's safety video recommended before starting. The soap starts fairly soft due to the aloe and high water content and cures to a lovely texture after 1-2 months of drying. For a more rustic hot process bar usable within a couple of weeks, use only 150g water with 30-50g aloe gel. The recipe can be made without aloe as a basic beginner hot process recipe. Author calculates recipe volumes to fit the chosen mould and recommends running any recipe through a lye calculator first.
ingredients_published: 225g rice bran oil (or substitute more olive oil)
200g filtered tap water (half ice; 150g for a harder soap)

Almond Meal Soap.detailed_instructions:
1. Put on protective gear - goggles and gloves (long sleeves, long pants, socks recommended so no skin is exposed).
2. Weigh the liquid oils - pour 18 oz olive oil and 1 oz castor oil into the slow cooker.
3. Weigh 4.9 oz lye (sodium hydroxide) into a ceramic or glass bowl (plastic is staticky and lye beads stick to it).
4. Weigh 11 oz distilled water into a 32 oz heatproof glass measuring cup; the author used a mix of distilled-water ice cubes and water to reduce fumes and cooling time.
5. Pour the lye slowly into the water and stir to dissolve - this generates a lot of heat and fumes; a cold water bath in the sink also helps cooling. NEVER pour water into lye: the reaction can splash/erupt and cause serious injury. Set the lye water aside to cool.
6. Weigh the solid fats - 8 oz coconut oil, 6 oz palm oil, 2 oz shea butter - into a second 32 oz glass measuring cup and melt in the microwave: 1 minute first, then 30-second increments as needed.
7. Pour the melted solid fats into the olive and castor oil in the slow cooker and mix.
8. Pour the lye water slowly and carefully into the oils while stirring.
9. Stick blend until the mixture reaches a thin pudding/gravy consistency - drippings from the lifted blender should leave patterns on the surface rather than disappearing. Alternative trace check: the mixture's temperature rises a couple of degrees F at trace (tip credited to 'Smart Soapmaking' by Anne L. Watson). Pulse the blender every 5-10 seconds; trace can take under a minute to a few minutes.
10. Once traced, set the cooker to LOW, put the lid on, and wait. After 15 minutes check that the mixture has not separated into oil and lye water; if it has, stir it back together with a spatula.
11. Check again after another 20-30 minutes - the outside edge starts turning translucent, progressing toward the center.
12. When much of the mixture is translucent, stir with a spatula and continue cooking; stir again in 20-30 minutes. At some point it looks like apple sauce. An oil-like layer on the surface is glycerin produced during saponification - just stir it back in.
13. After 1.5-2 hours of cooking and stirring the soap has a Vaseline-like consistency; the oils and lye are fully saponified and the soap is neutral. Turn off the slow cooker.
14. Add 5-6 tbsp almond meal and mix well with a spatula, then add 1 tbsp intense almond fragrance oil and mix well. Guideline: 1-2 tbsp fragrance oil per 2 lb of oils; hot process needs less fragrance than cold process because the lye is already neutralized when it is added.
15. Scoop the soap into the mold, banging the mold on the counter while filling so the thick soap fills all edges and corners. Work quickly - a skin forms as it cools and additional soap won't stick to it. The top is rarely smooth; trim after unmolding if desired.
16. Once cool and firm, remove from the mold and cut. The soap can be used immediately since it is already neutral; for longer-lasting, harder bars let them dry a couple of weeks.
Almond Meal Soap.extra_notes: Yield: ~3 lbs of soap; all measurements are by weight, not volume. Equipment cautions: never use nonstick, aluminum, cast iron, or tin pots/utensils (they react badly with lye); wood not recommended for repeated use. No preservatives - store bars in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight and use within about a year (six months in hot, humid areas). Cleanup: fill the crock with water to dissolve residue, then (with goggles/gloves on) wipe tools down and wash with dishwashing liquid and warm water. Tools list includes: digital scale reading to 0.25 oz with tare, instant-read thermometer, 3-qt stainless bowl, two 32 oz heatproof glass cups, stick blender, 4-qt slow cooker, lined or greased mold.
ingredients_published: 1 tbsp intense almond fragrance oil (Majestic Mountain Sage)

Simple Natural Homemade Soap.detailed_instructions:
1. Make the lye solution: wearing gloves and goggles, weigh 4.5 oz (128g) distilled water into a stainless steel or heavy-duty plastic pitcher (never aluminum - it reacts adversely with lye). Weigh 2.14 oz (60g) lye into a small cup, then sprinkle the lye into the water (never water into lye or you can get a lye volcano) and gently stir with a heavy-duty plastic or silicone utensil until fully dissolved. The solution gets very hot - work near an open window, outside, or under an exhaust fan and avoid breathing the fumes (a mask is suggested for sensitive lungs). Set aside somewhere undisturbed to cool for 30-40 minutes before mixing with the oils.
2. Weigh and heat the oils: weigh 2.5 oz coconut oil and melt in a double boiler or over low heat. Weigh 12 oz olive oil and 1.5 oz castor oil into a heat-resistant soaping pot or pitcher. Pour the hot melted coconut oil into the other oils, bringing the mix to roughly 90-100F (32-38C).
3. Combine and mix to trace: pour the lye solution into the warm oils. With a stick/immersion blender (not a handheld mixer), stir with the motor OFF ~30 seconds, then blend with the motor ON for 30-60 seconds; keep alternating motor-off stirring and motor-on blending (running it continuously risks burning out the motor and adding air bubbles) until trace - the batter is thick enough to leave an imprint when drizzled across the surface. Optional: stir in about 1 tbsp (15 ml) lavender, lemongrass, geranium (rose), or peppermint essential oil now for a light scent after cure.
4. Pour into the mold (cold process - no added heat). Cover gently with a sheet of freezer paper, then a blanket or towel to hold in heat. Check occasionally: a crack down the middle means it is too hot - move it somewhere cooler. Color changes and a translucent jelly-like texture (especially in the middle) are normal gel phase. After 24 hours remove paper and towel; leave uncovered in the mold 2-3 more days until firm enough to release easily.
5. Cure: unmold the loaf, slice into bars, and cure in open air at least 4-6 weeks to evaporate excess water so bars are harder and longer lasting. High-olive soaps like this benefit from 6-8+ weeks, getting harder and milder with age. Store finished soap in a cool area away from heat, sunlight, and humidity.
Simple Natural Homemade Soap.extra_notes: Yield: 4 bars, almost 1.5 lb (16 oz oil + 2.14 oz lye + 4.5 oz water = 22.64 oz), using a small 4-inch silicone loaf mold. 6% superfat. All measurements by weight - an accurate scale is required. If allergic to coconut oil, substitute 2.5 oz (71g) babassu oil. The recipe deliberately uses a steeper-than-usual water discount because high olive oil soaps take longer to firm up and cure; less water speeds this and eases mold release. Designed for beginners and people with multiple skin sensitivities.
ingredients_published: 2.5 oz (71 g) (15.6%) coconut oil (substitute babassu oil if allergic)
2.14 oz (60 g) food grade lye (6% superfat)
Optional: ~1 tbsp (15 ml) essential oil (lavender, lemongrass, geranium, or peppermint)

Old Faithful.detailed_instructions:
1. This page publishes the formula only (no step-by-step method): 32% coconut oil, 32% palm oil, 32% olive oil, 4% castor oil, superfatted at 5%.
2. Described as simple and reliable, great for beginners; the castor oil gives a luscious lather; similar to Bramble Berry's Lots of Lather Quick Mix.
Old Faithful.extra_notes: The source page is a formulating guide, not a tutorial - it lists tried-and-true oil-percentage recipes (all 5% superfat) plus general rules: start with balanced ratios like 34/33/33 (olive/coconut/palm) or 30/30/30/10; liquid oils trace more slowly (good for intricate designs, softer bars); hard oils trace faster and give firmer bars that unmold sooner; only olive or coconut are recommended for 100% single-oil soaps; oils can be substituted (e.g. canola or rice bran for olive) but recipes must be recalculated through a lye calculator. No batch size, water amount, temperatures, or cure time are given on the page.

Alpine Swirl Cold Process Soap.detailed_instructions:
1. COLORANT PREP: Disperse 1 tsp titanium dioxide into 1 tbsp lightweight liquid oil (sunflower or sweet almond); in separate containers disperse 1 tsp Cobalt Blue Mica and 1 tsp Stormy Blue Mica each into 1 tbsp lightweight liquid oil; use a mini mixer to remove clumps. Optional: micronize the titanium dioxide in a coffee grinder first so no white streaks show in the final soap.
2. FRAGRANCE PREP: Measure 1.75 oz Fresh Snow Fragrance Oil into a glass, fragrance-safe container; set aside.
3. SAFETY FIRST: Goggles, gloves, and long sleeves; keep kids, pets, distractions, and tripping hazards away from the soaping space; always soap in a well-ventilated area.
4. Slowly and carefully add 4.9 oz lye to 10.4 oz distilled water; stir gently until fully dissolved; set aside to cool. Optional for a harder bar that releases faster: add sodium lactate to the cooled lye water at 1 tsp per pound of oils - 2 tsp for this recipe.
5. Melt and combine 3.5 oz avocado oil, 1 oz castor oil, 8.8 oz coconut oil, 8.8 oz olive oil, 8.8 oz palm oil (fully melt the whole palm container before portioning), and 4.2 oz rice bran oil in a large bowl. When lye water and oils are at 130F or below and ideally within 10 degrees of each other, add the lye water to the oils and stick blend to a very thin trace.
6. Split the soap into 3 containers and whisk in colors: Container A (300 mL): 1.5 tsp dispersed Stormy Blue Mica; Container B (300 mL): 2 tsp dispersed Cobalt Blue Mica; Container C (remaining soap): all the dispersed titanium dioxide.
7. Add the 1.75 oz Fresh Snow Fragrance Oil proportionally to each container (okay to eyeball) and whisk in.
8. Pour a small amount of white soap into the mold - just enough to cover the bottom. Then alternate pouring small amounts of dark blue, white, and light blue at varying heights so the soap drops to different areas instead of layering (drop swirl). Pouring white between the two blues helps define the swirls; precision is not needed.
9. Continue pouring until the mold is filled, saving a very small amount of each color for the top.
10. Insert the Hanger Swirl Tool down one side of the mold and swirl with loop-de-loop motions - mix big and small loops and vary horizontal/vertical direction for a more complex swirl. After about 7-10 swirls, remove the tool up and out on one side of the mold.
11. Pour or plop dollops of the remaining soap on top (trace may be quite thick by now); placement need not be exact.
12. Use the back of a spoon to create peaks and divots in the top, then sprinkle Luna UltraSparkle Mica on top for added sparkle.
13. Spritz the top with 99% isopropyl alcohol. The makers set the mold on a heating pad for about 1 hour to promote gel phase. Leave in the mold 1-3 days (depending on whether sodium lactate was used), unmold, cut into bars, and cure 4-6 weeks.
Alpine Swirl Cold Process Soap.extra_notes: Level: Intermediate. Time: 1 hour. Yield: 3 pounds of soap. Uses a 10-inch silicone loaf mold and Hanger Swirl Tool; 10% water discount is built into the 10.4 oz water amount. Scent notes: heliotrope, sparkling icicle, vetiver, sandalwood (Fresh Snow FO). Isopropyl alcohol spritz prevents soda ash. Tutorial photography: Amanda Kerzman.
ingredients_published: Titanium Dioxide (1 tsp, dispersed in 1 tbsp oil)
Cobalt Blue Mica (1 tsp, dispersed in 1 tbsp oil)
Stormy Blue Mica (1 tsp, dispersed in 1 tbsp oil)

Carrot Cold Process Soap.detailed_instructions:
1. SCULPTING TOOL PREP: Cut sturdy cardboard into a T shape whose top arms rest level on the mold rails; draw and cut out a carrot shape (theirs ~2.5 inches from bottom to top; exact size flexible). Wrap the tool in clear packaging tape to make it stronger and soap-proof.
2. MOLD PREP: Line the Tall Narrow Wood Loaf Mold with freezer paper, shiny side up.
3. FRAGRANCE PREP: Measure 2 oz Avocado Fragrance Oil and 0.6 oz Orange 10X Essential Oil into separate small glass containers.
4. COLORANT PREP: Disperse 1 tsp brown oxide into 1 tbsp lightweight liquid oil (sunflower/sweet almond), and 1 tsp Nuclear Orange Pigment into 1 tbsp lightweight liquid oil; mini-mix out clumps. Keep 2 tbsp walnut shells and 2 tsp orange peel powder nearby.
5. SAFETY FIRST: Goggles, gloves, long sleeves; kids/pets/distractions out; well-ventilated area.
6. Slowly and carefully add 5.6 oz lye to 13.2 oz distilled water; stir gently until dissolved and clear; set aside to cool. Optional sodium lactate in the cooled lye water at 1 tsp per pound of oils (2.5 tsp here) for a harder, faster-releasing bar.
7. Melt and combine 2 oz carrot seed oil, 1.2 oz castor oil, 2.4 oz deodorized cocoa butter, 10 oz coconut oil, 13.6 oz olive oil, and 10.8 oz palm oil (fully melt and mix the whole palm container before portioning) in a large bowl.
8. Once the lye water has cooled to about 130F, split off 10 oz of the oil mixture into a separate container, and carefully (safety gear on) pour off 4.7 oz of the lye solution into another container - these two will later be mixed to form the orange carrot soap.
9. Slowly add the large batch of lye solution to the large batch of oils and stick blend to thin trace.
10. Add the 2 oz Avocado Fragrance Oil and stick blend in.
11. Add all the dispersed brown oxide and 2 tbsp walnut shells; whisk in thoroughly.
12. At thin-medium trace (pulse the stick blender a few times if still thin), pour all the brown soap into the mold and tap firmly on the counter to release bubbles.
13. Wait for the brown soap to firm: it must hold its shape yet still scrape out smoothly. Test every ~3 minutes by scraping a small amount off the very top with the carrot tool; about 8-10 minutes worked for them, but timing varies. Start sooner rather than later - too thin can wait longer, but too thick cannot be undone.
14. Insert the cardboard carrot tool and pull it through the mold, placing scraped-out soap into a spare mold. The first passes are awkward and messy - that is okay.
15. Keep sliding the tool down the mold, lifting it out to discard excess soap, until about three-fourths of the way; keep the tool tracking the same line or the carrot gets very wide.
16. Near the far end, reverse direction; keep moving the tool back and forth until it no longer catches soap.
17. Mix the reserved lye and oils: pour the lye into the oils and stick blend to thin trace.
18. Add the 0.6 oz Orange 10X Essential Oil and blend in.
19. Add 1.5 tsp dispersed Nuclear Orange Pigment and 2 tsp orange peel powder; whisk in.
20. Gently pour the orange soap into the carved negative space until level with the top of the brown soap.
21. Let any leftover orange soap thicken slightly, then pour it down the middle of the orange layer to build up the center.
22. Smooth the orange soap with a small spoon into a rounded top (perfection not needed). Set aside while prepping the frosting batch.
23. FROSTING - PREP: Suit up again (goggles, gloves, long sleeves, ventilation). Cut the tip off a disposable frosting bag and insert the 1M frosting tip. Disperse 1 tsp Green Chrome Oxide Pigment into 1 tbsp lightweight liquid oil.
24. FROSTING - Slowly add 1.8 oz lye to 4.3 oz distilled water, stir until dissolved and clear, cool (optional 1 tsp sodium lactate).
25. FROSTING - Melt and combine 0.7 oz carrot seed oil, 0.4 oz castor oil, 0.8 oz deodorized cocoa butter, 3.3 oz coconut oil, 4.4 oz olive oil, 3.5 oz palm oil.
26. FROSTING - When the lye water is about 130F, add it slowly to the oils and stick blend to thin trace.
27. FROSTING - Whisk in 1/2 tsp dispersed Chrome Green Oxide; split off 200-300 mL into a separate container; add 1.5 tsp more dispersed green to the larger container for a darker green; stick blend both containers to thick trace. (The published directions were altered from the photos to reduce leftover soap.)
28. Plop light green soap on top of the brown on both sides of the mold and smooth with a spoon.
29. Spoon dollops of dark green (plus leftover light green) into the frosting bag, twist closed, and pipe dollops of soap on top of the orange down the whole length of the mold.
30. Repeat the piping 2-3 more times to build height; put leftover green soap into a spare mold.
31. Spritz the top with 99% isopropyl alcohol to prevent soda ash. They left the soap uncovered at room temperature; it gelled and developed glycerin rivers, which suited the dirt design. To prevent gel phase instead, refrigerate or freeze for 5-24 hours. Leave in the mold 2-3 days to harden, unmold, cut into bars, and cure fully for 4-6 weeks.
Carrot Cold Process Soap.extra_notes: Makes 4 pounds of soap; total time about 3 hours; sculpted-layer / negative-space technique (similar to their Horse Sculpted Layers tutorial). The base uses one lye batch and one oil batch split 25%/75% so the brown soap can harden while the orange stays fluid; the green frosting is a separate third batch. Beginners are told to stop and learn CP basics and lye safety first (free SoapQueen.tv 4-part series). Superfat implied by percentages; base oils blend: carrot seed 5%, castor 3%, cocoa butter 6%, coconut 25%, olive 34%, palm 27% (same percentages for the frosting batch).
ingredients_published: Soap base: 2 oz Carrot Seed Oil (5%)
Soap base: 2.4 oz Deodorized Cocoa Butter (6%)
Soap base: 5.6 oz Sodium Hydroxide Lye
Soap base: 2 oz Avocado Fragrance Oil
Soap base: 0.6 oz Orange 10X Essential Oil
Soap base: Nuclear Orange Pigment, Brown Oxide, Walnut Shells (2 tbsp), Orange Peel Powder (2 tsp)
Frosting: Green Chrome Pigment Oxide, Disposable Frosting Bag, 1M Frosting Tip
Tall Narrow Wood Loaf Mold; 99% isopropyl alcohol

Marseille Soap.detailed_instructions:
1. The thread itself publishes no instructions in the page text: the actual recipe (from the book 'Soap Naturally' by Patrizia Garzena and Marina Tadiello) was posted as a PDF attachment ('010420 Marseille Soap.pdf', 96.4 KB), and XenForo attachment downloads require a forum login - the file is not reachable as a guest.
2. Context visible in the thread: the recipe description calls it a laundry soap, and the original poster's comments indicate it is roughly a 50/50 olive oil and tallow soap.
3. Forum members add traditional background: authentic savon de Marseille is 100% olive oil, made by hot process, with the soap paste washed with brine to remove glycerin - effectively a 0% superfat, glycerin-free castile suited to household/laundry use rather than bathing.
Marseille Soap.extra_notes: Page loads fine (HTTP 200) but the recipe content is login-gated, so treated as paywalled. Historical notes from the thread: a 1688 French law required olive oil only; the name is no longer regulated; suggested tweaks from members include adding beer or 1-2% sugar (of total oil weight) to boost lather. Recovering the full instructions would require a forum account or the 'Soap Naturally' book.

Rustic Clay Soap.detailed_instructions:
1. Calculate the recipe with a soap calculator (SoapCalc) for your batch size to get finite amounts of fats, lye, and water: 55% liquid oils, 20% beef tallow, 20% refined (RBD) coconut oil, 5% castor oil; 5% superfat; 'Water as % of Oils' set to 30%. Per 500g of fats also weigh 10g white kaolin clay, 5g sodium lactate, and 5g French green clay.
2. Put on safety gear: gloves and eye protection; an apron is a good idea.
3. Prepare the mould (author used a wooden loaf mould; a cavity mould also works).
4. Melt the oils together in the soaping pot and let them cool to slightly warmer than room temperature. Mix the lye water (use ice for part of the water to speed cooling) and let it cool to about room temperature.
5. When both lye solution and melted fats are slightly warmer than room temperature: blend the kaolin clay into the fats and stir the sodium lactate into the lye water.
6. Gently pour the lye mixture into the melted fats and bring the batter to a thin trace.
7. At thin trace, pour about 1/4-1/3 of the batter into a second container and blend the French green clay into that portion.
8. Pour the kaolin (uncoloured) batter into the loaf mould and knock the mould on the countertop to even it out and release bubbles.
9. Gently spoon the green batter on top, smooth it, and sculpt the top as desired (author made a mohawk ridge with a spatula). Leave to saponify.
10. After about 36 hours the soap should be firm enough to slice. With a silicone mould, freeze the loaf before unmoulding to prevent denting (unnecessary for a deconstructable brittle mould). Unmould, trim any dangly bits, and slice - a wire slicer (e.g. a cheese slicer) is recommended over a knife, which drags stickily.
11. Leave the bars to age/dry for 3-4 weeks before using.
Rustic Clay Soap.extra_notes: Formula is given as percentages plus per-500g-fats additions, to be run through SoapCalc (5% superfat, water 30% of oils). The author's own liquid-oil blend for this batch included olive oil (26.67%) and safflower oil (27.4%); the high safflower content raised the iodine value, making softer, shorter-lived bars - she recommends olive and rice bran oil for the liquid portion instead of replicating her blend. Kaolin clay gives a creamy appearance and lather; French green clay colours the top layer (French pink/yellow clay or a smaller amount of mica are alternatives; beware strongly pigmented clays that can bleed). Lather is creamy and low. Shelf life: bar soap is self-preserving (low water, high pH, anionic surfactant); bars last years if allowed to dry between uses - discard if orange spots (rancidity/DOS) appear.
ingredients_published: 55% liquid oils (author's batch: olive oil 26.67% + safflower oil 27.4%; olive/rice bran recommended)
Lye and water calculated to 5% superfat, water at 30% of oils

The Beginner's Guide to Making CP Soap.detailed_instructions:
1. Make your recipe: choose a few simple oils and a batch size of no more than 1-3 pounds while learning. Run the oil amounts through an online lye calculator; the guide recommends a 5% lye discount (superfat) and a 33% lye solution (twice as much water as lye) for beginners. Print the calculator results and keep them at hand.
2. Prepare the space: work uninterrupted on a flat surface with access to heat and a sink; keep small children and animals away - lye is caustic. Protect or cover the work surface (stainless steel is best; do not soap on granite or quartz countertops - one splatter will ruin them).
3. Prepare yourself: put on apron, goggles, and gloves. Lye and raw soap are painful on skin and worse in an eye.
4. Make the lye solution: tare a heavy plastic, heat-resistant glass, or stainless container on the scale; SLOWLY weigh in the distilled water accurately. Separately tare and weigh the sodium hydroxide. In a well-ventilated area SLOWLY pour the sodium hydroxide into the water - NEVER pour water into sodium hydroxide. Mix well with a spatula, avoiding the fumes. The solution heats up; set it aside to cool to between 95F and 105F. CAUTION: if lye gets on skin, flush with cool water immediately.
5. While the lye cools, prepare fragrance (optional), colorants (optional), other additives, and the mold.
6. Mix and melt the oils: tare and weigh each oil/fat separately (scoop solids, pour liquids), adding each to the stainless soap pot. Melt solid fats over medium heat without leaving the pot unattended - gently melt, don't overheat or burn, stirring to break up solid pieces. Turn off the heat and let the oils cool to 95-105F.
7. Measure remaining ingredients while everything cools. Rule of thumb: no more than about 0.6 oz of fragrance per 1 lb of oils.
8. Make the soap: confirm oil and lye temperatures with a digital thermometer; have mold, oils, lye solution, additives, and stick blender ready, safety gear back on. Pour the lye solution slowly into the fats/oils while stirring with a whisk; scrape sides and stir with a spatula until initially blended.
9. Fully submerge the stick blender (tilt the pot if needed) and blend in short bursts, reaching edges and bottom, scraping down the sides so no unmixed lye or oil remains. Hand mixing also works but takes much longer.
10. Blend until 'trace': thin enough to pour off a spoon, thick enough to leave a trace on the surface as it falls back in - about like cake batter.
11. At trace, add fragrance, color, and/or other additives, incorporating fully with whisk or stick blender.
12. Slowly pour the wet soap into the mold, getting it into all corners; tap the mold lightly on the work surface to settle the soap and release trapped air.
13. Wrap or cover the mold with a heavy blanket or towel to contain the heat and let it rest 12-24 hours; it warms up (saponification) and then cools. Unmold once fully cooled.
14. The soap may still be soft when unmolded; let it rest 1-3 days until hardened a bit, then cut as desired. Set bars aside in a cool area with good air circulation for 4-6 weeks until fully hard.
The Beginner's Guide to Making CP Soap.extra_notes: Process spans 1-3 days plus a 4-6 week cure. Equipment list: safety goggles, rubber gloves, paper mask (for lye fumes); scale reading to 1/10th; pyrex or stainless mixing containers; spatulas, spoon, whisk; stainless pot; accurate quick-read thermometer; small cups for additives; apron (optional); stick blender (optional but faster); soap mold. Footnotes: 5% lye discount eliminates any chance of a lye-heavy bar from saponification-value variation; 33% lye solution is easiest to work with (50% solutions are an advanced technique; 25% solutions take a long time and suit tricky multi-color soaps). Never use aluminum. No specific oil formula is prescribed - the reader chooses oils and runs the lye calculator.
ingredients_published: Oils or fats of your choice (run through a lye calculator before starting)
Fragrance oil or essential oil (optional, max ~0.6 oz per lb of oils)

Calendula, Chamomile, and Comfrey Soap.detailed_instructions:
1. Prepare the lye using cold chamomile tea in place of water (same procedure as with water); set aside until the temperature comes down to about 100F.
2. Combine all the oils (2/3 cup olive, 2/3 cup coconut, 2/3 cup vegetable oil blend) and heat just enough to melt the coconut oil, until the mixture reaches about 100F.
3. Slowly mix the lye solution into the oils and stir for 5 minutes.
4. After 5 minutes, keep stirring by hand or use an immersion blender until the mixture thickens like pudding - this is trace.
5. At trace, add 1 tsp dried calendula petals, 1 tsp dried chamomile flowers, and 1 tsp dried ground comfrey root or leaves. All plant material MUST be dried - fresh material can cause spoilage in the soap.
6. Stir well to incorporate and pour into molds.
7. Remove from the molds after 24 hours; cut into smaller bars if a large mold was used.
8. Cure for 3-4 weeks.
Calendula, Chamomile, and Comfrey Soap.extra_notes: Described as a perennial favorite - soothing and healing, with just enough herbal matter for gentle exfoliation. NOTE: unusually for soap making, this source publishes the recipe in VOLUME measurements (cups), not weights - including '1/4 cup lye' - which differs from our stored version if it uses weights; the page links to the author's lye-safety article. The same page carries sibling recipes (Oatmeal Milk & Honey; Gardener's/Mechanic's) using the same base pattern: 2/3 cup each of three oils, 3/4 cup liquid, 1/4 cup lye, trace additions, 24 h unmold, 3-4 week cure.
